newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan retailers post mixed results in tough times.
newsitem.headline: Japan retailers post mixed results in tough times.

text.p: Earnings results from several of Japan's big retailers presented a mixed picture on Friday, with profits attributable largely to cost-cutting and other special factors rather than any recovery in withered consumer demand.

Consumption has yet to return to full strength in the face of a slow economic recovery, and company officials added that they were worried about slack consumer demand in the current business year after Japan's sales tax was increased on April 1.

Leading department store operators such as Mitsukoshi Ltd and Takashimaya Co Ltd enjoyed parent current profit growth of 92 percent and 55.2 percent, respectively, in the fiscal year which ended on February 28.
But weak consumer sentiment hit Japan's largest retail chain operator hard, forcing Daiei Inc into the red on a group basis.

Daiei, which operates a nationwide network of supermarkets, said it suffered a group new loss of 11.9 billion yen ($94.4 million) in fiscal 1996/97 after posting a net profit of 5.08 billion yen ($40.3 million) in 1995/96.

Mitsukoshi posted parent current profit of 10.70 billion yen ($84.9 million) in 1996/97. It attributed the rise to sales-promotion activity and cost-cutting, though sales grew a scant 1.4 percent to 767.19 billion ($6.08 billion), the first rise in three years.

Takashimaya posted a parent current profit of 15.94 billion yen ($126 million) in 1996/97, with its sales growing 22.6 percent to 1.09 trillion ($8.6 billion), helped by robust sales at its new store in central Tokyo's bustling Shinjuku district.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses made on investments.

Takashimaya president Tatsuo Tanaka told reporters that sales at the store hit 41.3 billion yen ($327 million) by the end of February from its October opening, higher than its forecast of 35 billion yen ($277 million).
The store is in a huge 11-floor shopping mall which also houses large book and music stores, an indoor amusement park, beauty parlours and a 3-D theatre.
Tanaka said sales at the new store should grow to 87.7 billion yen ($696 million) in the current full business year, but added that the overall environment was not very rosy.
"With the rise in the sales tax and the abolition of income tax cuts this year, we can hardly say our business environment is good," he said.
The government increased the sales tax to five percent from three percent and abolished the income tax cuts on April 1.

Daiei said it suffered a 98 percent nosedive in its parent current profit, hit by reduced food sales resulting from a food-poisoning epidemic which swept Japan last year, as well as sluggish sales of seasonal goods.
However, it predicted that the group would return to profit in 1997/98, although analysts said the road ahead was bumpy.
Another supermarket chain operator, Ito-Yokado Co Ltd, suffered a 9.0 percent slide in its parent current profit to 69.65 billion yen ($552 million).
While many retailers cited concerns about the weak consumer demand, convenience store chains shrugged off such fears and posted robust growth in sales and profits in 1996/97.

On Thursday, Seven-Eleven Japan Co Ltd announced a 7.2 percent rise in its parent current profit to 105.15 billion yen ($834 million), making it the first retailer in Japan ever to post profit of more than 100 billion yen ($793 million).
It retained the status as the biggest Japanese retailer in terms of profits for a fourth straight year, easily surpassing that of Ito-Yokado, its parent company.
Seven-Eleven said its operating revenues, which include sales at directly managed stores, grew 8.9 percent due to healthy food sales and an expansion of its franchise network.
